newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Bundesbank utters strong words on inflation.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bundesbank utters strong words on inflation.

text.p: The German Bundesbank sounded alarm bells on monetary policy on Wednesday, making clear it was scrutinising a recent upturn in inflation and would not hesitate to tighten its policy if warranted.
In its August monthly report, the central bank said: "It cannot be overlooked that there has been a stronger rise in consumer prices in the last few months."
"The Bundesbank will orientate its policy in such a way that price stability, which has been essentially achieved, can be maintained," it added.
The comments landed in financial markets already dominated by expectations that a German interest rate rise -- signalling the end of five years of easier policy -- is in the pipeline.
The mark gained in response to the comments and German bonds and shares -- already concerned by the prospect of an interest rate rise in the United States -- were trading lower.
"We had been expecting an increase at the end of the year," said economist Marco Kramer at Paribas Capital Markets.
"But I share the feeling that the way is now being paved for an earlier move. We now think there will be an interest rate rise in the next three months," he added.

Recent sharp slides in the mark had been seen by markets as the main reason spurring the Bundesbank to action. The dollar has gained about 20 percent against the mark this year despite repeated warnings along the way that it had risen far enough.
But the new element of tough talk on inflation puts the speculation into a completely different category.

The Bundesbank regularly stresses that it does not follow an exchange-rate-oriented policy but rather sticks religiously to its main task of defending the price stability of the mark, changing its policy when justified on domestic grounds.
In interviews published last week, the central bank's chief economist Otmar Issing had pointed to high capacity utilisation and price pressures at various levels of the economy.
Yet economists believe an immediate move is unlikely, gambling that the price pressures within the economy would have to gain strength before eliciting a response.
Annual inflation hit a 25-month high of 1.9 percent in July, but was distorted higher by special factors.

The central bank already refrained from adjusting its main money-market rate, the repo, this week, leading financial markets to expect no policy change until the Bundesbank council resumes regular meetings on August 21, after the summer break.
In its report, the Bundesbank repeated recent comments that it was watching the currency markets closely, linking this firmly to the potential influence of mark losses on prices.

"The Bundesbank will observe further currency rate developments closely with a view to the risks presented for price stability," it said. A weaker currency holds the risk of imported inflation as import prices are boosted.
Turning to domestic political issues, the Bundesbank urged the political parties to find a way to break a stalemate preventing a much-needed tax reform from taking place.
"Only large, sweeping tax reform can lead out of this dead end," the bank's report said.

It also warned that the German government's 1997 income from taxes would probably be even lower than the last official estimate showed. Bonn's finance ministry responded quickly that it saw no need make any revision to its figures.

"From the current standpoint, tax receipts for 1997 will probably still be lower than the May forecast," the report said. That estimate showed tax receipts this year were likely to be 18 billion marks less than the original prediction.

The fresh estimates were seen as a heavy blow to the government , which is battling to cut its budget deficits to make the grade for entry into Europe's common currency, due for launch on January 1, 1999.
Government plans to reform Germany's convoluted tax system were thwarted last month when opposition Social Democrats blocked a bill proposing 30 billion marks of tax cuts.
